item.title: Making Chicken Transparent Using Dorito Dust (239 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://chillphysicsenjoyer.substack.com/p/making-chicken-transparent-using, See on Hacker News

Thank you Adaobi for such a wonderful suggestion. All credit to her for the idea, we are still workin’ on it!

My genius friend Adaobi Adibe sent me a paper on making biological tissues transparent. In “Achieving optical transparency in live animals with absorbing molecules”, the authors make biological tissues, like chicken breast, transparent by soaking them in a solution of tartrazine. Tartrazine is the very bright yellowish-orange food dye that is found on Doritos.

We aim to do a more ambitious replication imminently. But as a warm up, I tried to replicate parts of this protocol by soaking chicken breast in tartrazine solution. I got partial transparency but not to the degree of the paper. The sample below is an approximately 2mm thick raw chicken breast cut from a 5mm slice that was soaked in ~0.19 M tartrazine solution for 6 hours at room temperature. I took an image of this with a desk light. You can see the grid lines showing through from underneath. The chicken, even though the texture to the touch is the same, has a visual quality like that of gummy bears.

The original paper used 0.62 M, 40 °C and a machine shaker, but I couldn't find a way to do this safely, nor did I have the equipment to do so. Hence the altered protocol.

The image below is a different angle of my sample. The sample on the left is the same 2mm thick chicken breast slice as above. And the sample on the right is a control where I soaked it in water (it is slightly yellow since this process is super messy and I got dust on it).

In the top part of the sample we do see some transparency, with the 5mm x 5mm grid showing through. The visual quality of the chicken breast takes on a gummy-bear like quality. Kinda makes me wanna chew it if it wouldn't give me Salmonella.

I don't wanna get copyrighted by Doritos so here is a cartoon of where you can find tartrazine in the wild.

How does this work?

The current model we have is that the absorbance properties of the tartrazine also shift the refractive index of water. By pushing the refractive index of water to that of protein and lipid solution, we make the object more transparent. I’ll explain this in great detail later.

Tartrazine was from APC Pure. It was >80% dye content, which means some uncertainty over what the true molar concentration will be. I then prepared three concentrations of tartrazine at these molar concentrations, one of which was just a 0 concentration as a control.

  • Tartrazine: 0 g, Tap water: 20 g, w/w: 0%, Molality (mol/kg water): 0, Tartrazine (mmol): 0, Molarity (approx.): 0 M (control)

  • Tartrazine: 2 g, Tap water: 18 g, w/w: 10%, Molality (mol/kg water): 0.21, Tartrazine (mmol): 3.7, Molarity (approx.): ~0.19 M

  • Tartrazine: 6 g, Tap water: 14 g, w/w: 30%, Molality (mol/kg water): 0.80, Tartrazine (mmol): 11.2, Molarity (approx.): ~0.56 M

Tartrazine has M = 534.4 g/mol. Moles use the nominal mass (the powder is >80% dye, so true values are up to ~15% lower). Molarity assumes a final solution volume of ~20 mL.

This is what the tartrazine looked like. It doesn't have an odour, and it seems to be considered food safe by the FDA, so I didn't bother wearing gloves for this bit. Here is a picture of the tartrazine and the specs.

  • Product: Tartrazine E102 FG, C.I. 19140

  • Dye content: >80%

  • Molecular formula: C16H9N4Na3O9S2

  • Molecular weight: 534.37 g/mol

  • λmax (in water): 425 nm

  • Water-insoluble matter: <0.20%

  • Subsidiary dyes: <1.00%

  • Heavy metals (as Pb): <40 mg/kg

To prepare the solutions I used a jeweller's scale to weigh out the right amounts and then added tap water to the weights listed in the table.

To dissolve the tartrazine, I mixed it with a glass stirrer at room temperature until there were no visible lumps.¹

Here are the different solutions at different concentrations, the most concentrated one on the left, the middle concentration in the middle, and then a water control on the right.

Next, I got chicken breast fillets from Tesco. I cut a 5mm thick slab and then cut three pieces out to around 15mm in length.

I then soaked 5mm thick slices of chicken breast in each of the three solutions.

After 6 hours of soaking, these were the results.

First, the chicken in the highest concentration solution failed, because the tartrazine seemed to crystallise. This is what it looked like - it got all crusty.

For the middle concentration (~0.19 M), the chicken appeared gelatinous. But it wasn't transparent. The control chicken remained completely opaque.

I threw these pieces out and then tried again with the method below.

And then I tried again with the same procedure, with the aim of soaking it for 12 hours at room temperature. Given the issues with the highest concentration (~0.56 M), I only tried the water control and the middle concentration (~0.19 M). But this time I put the chicken in test tubes and covered it, given that I was gonna leave it out for 12 hours at room temperature. I wanted to mitigate the food safety risk.

This was the 12-hour-soaked piece. Whilst it's hard to see with the camera, there was some slight visible translucency compared to the control.

To examine it I put it under some light above.

I then cut approximately 2mm slices of chicken. This was quite fiddly to do with a small slimy piece. Here is what it looked like compared to the control.

This technique has been used to make fluorescence imaging much easier in live animals.

On my end, doing this well could add to the set of things that independent scientists could image at home. We might be able to probe internal structures of things more casually. Making things transparent would give better images and would allow independent scientists to look at tissue structure more closely.

Effective observation at low cost is one of the themes of my research. I wrote about writing tracing software for Brownian particles using my microscope in my last post. I am also thinking about trying to match the performance of CO2 gas sensing using pressure, which would make that type of sensing cheaper. In line with this theme, I’m super excited about attempting weird and cool techniques to make structures more easier to probe!

Here’s is more than you ever wanted to know about optical transparency.

A material can be opaque for two reasons. First, a material can absorb light and block it. Second, it can scramble light due to different refractive indices.

First, light rays from the other side could be absorbed when they pass through. If light is absorbed, the light can't hit your eyes and you can't see the other side. Light can have multiple wavelengths, and the wavelengths absorbed by the material are determined by the material's spectra. To calculate the spectra, we can approximate the physical behaviour of molecules to that of an electron around a potential. The Schrödinger equation tells us that this system can only occupy a discrete set of energies, and it tells us which ones these are. The differences between these energies set the wavelengths that are ultimately absorbed by the material.

In reality, materials are composed of lots of different things and so we expect them to also absorb different wavelengths.

Another reason for opacity is less obvious, but more interesting. The refractive index of a material tells us how quickly light travels within the medium. When light travels between materials with different refractive indices, it deflects slightly. When a material is packed with sub-materials that have different refractive indices, the refraction within causes light rays to get scattered since light rays ping around.

Biological materials contain a mix of different sub-materials inside - fibres, cells, proteins, and more. Each of these materials contains a different refractive index. When you have a material with one refractive index embedded in a material with a different refractive index, you get scattering. This scattering causes the light from the other side to get scrambled. The diagram below shows this.

We can model biological materials as a 'base material' of water, with chunks of lipids and proteins embedded inside, all of which have different refractive indices.

To make something transparent, we need to exploit the two causes of opacity. One approach is to try to change the absorbance spectra of a material so that it absorbs fewer wavelengths of light.

Alternatively (and this is the approach we'll cover in this post), we could try to change the refractive index of the water inside to match the embedded media. The image below shows this principle with biological tissues. If you can change the refractive index of water with a dye, you can then match it to the refractive index of proteins and lipids, which is slightly higher.

If you manage to do this without modifying the absorbance of a material, you should be able to make it more transparent.

Ok, so the game is to change the refractive index. Here is a map of the calculations we need to do to figure out how to modify the refractive index of a material.

To understand where the refractive index plays a part in a quantitative model, let's model how light travels according to Maxwell. Light is an electromagnetic wave, comprised of oscillating electric and magnetic waves. For this essay, let's focus on the electric field part to get the key intuitions.

Using complex representation, if light travels down the z axis, in a vacuum, we can write down the equation of light as the following. Because it's a wave, we can write

\(E(z, t) = E_0 \cos\!\left(\frac{\omega z}{c} - \omega t\right)\)

But for convenience we use complex numbers

\(E(z, t) = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ E_0\, e^{\,i\omega z / c \;-\; i\omega t} \right\}\)

Where E₀ is the amplitude (how strong the field is), ω is the angular frequency (at a fixed point the field goes round once every T = 2π/ω), c is the speed of light, z is distance along the beam and t is time. Crest to crest, the wavelength is λ = 2πc/ω.

In media though, we expect both the speed of light to change in the medium, as well as some absorption. We can rewrite the equation as follows

\(E(z, t) = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ E_0\, e^{\,i(n' + i\kappa)\,\omega z / c \;-\; i\omega t} \right\} = \mathrm{Re}\left\{ E_0\, e^{-\kappa \omega z / c}\, e^{\,i(n' \omega z / c \;-\; \omega t)} \right\}\)

The coefficient in the exponential n′ is a multiplier behind the spatial term, and represents the real refractive index. κ represents how much the wave attenuates, and is meant to denote absorption.

In practice we can group n′ + iκ as one number, and then refer to this as the complex refractive index.

First we need to try to change the real refractive index. If we can increase the refractive index of water to match the tissue refractive index, we would have a more transparent material. Water has a refractive index of 1.33. And although this number is variable, protein and lipid rich structures have a refractive index of around 1.45. So the game is to adjust the refractive index of the water around it towards 1.45, which would make it more transparent.

Whatever we do to the water, we also need to make sure that we don't make the absorbance property too high. If κ gets too high, then we'd end up absorbing all the light and it won't go transparent.

So how do we shift the refractive index? To understand refractive indices, we first need to understand polarisation. To first order, a material consists of electrons bound to nuclei. When an electric field is applied to a material, the relative positions of the electrons to their nuclei change.

from [http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/electric/dielec.html#c1]

For a positively charged particle and a negatively charged particle, polarisation is the magnitude of that charge multiplied by the displacement of one from the other. To calculate the polarisation, we need to model how far electrons displace from the nucleus under the electric field.

Electric fields provide a force on charges that are free. To model the effect of an electric field on a material, we treat the positive nucleus as fixed, and the electrons as free. To calculate the effect of the system, we'll use the Lorentz oscillator model.

In this model, the electrons are modelled to be bound to the nucleus like a damped spring, with the electric field applying a forcing. We can solve it exactly how we would solve a damped spring problem:

Newton's second law for the electron, with the light's field oscillating at ω:

\(m\ddot{x} = -m\omega_0^2\, x \;-\; m\gamma\,\dot{x} \;-\; e\,E_0\, e^{-i\omega t}\)

If we try an Ansatz for the position of the electron x(t) = x₀ e^(−iωt) (the electron oscillates at the driving frequency), we get that the position of the electron relative to the nucleus is given by the following expression.

\(x(t) = \frac{-e/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\; E(t)\)

The dipole moment is p = −ex, and with N electrons per unit volume the polarisation per unit volume is

\(\mathbf{P} = N p = \frac{N e^2/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\; \mathbf{E}\)

In this setup, ω₀ represents the natural frequency of the bound electron, which is the frequency the molecule absorbs at (for tartrazine, the 425 nm peak), γ represents the damping rate, which sets how broad that absorption peak is, and ω is the frequency of the electric field. Now we've found polarisation, we want to relate it to the refractive index itself. To do that, we need to do some gymnastics with two identities.

By convention, the polarisation can be written as proportional to the electric field

\(\mathbf{P} = \varepsilon_0\,\chi\,\mathbf{E}\)

where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space, χ is the electric susceptibility (a dimensionless number that says how easily the material polarises), and E is the electric field. Comparing with the Lorentz oscillator result above,

\(\chi(\omega) = \frac{N e^2/(\varepsilon_0 m)}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega}\)

To relate our polarisation, and electric susceptibility to the refractive index, we use the following trick. The below is an AI-assisted proof with manual checking.

This degree of polarisation and the electric field is encoded in something called the electric displacement field D. And the relationship between D and the electric field is linear, with the coefficient called the relative permittivity, εᵣ. P here represents the polarisation per unit volume, and is the average induced dipole moment across all of the material.

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mathbf{E} = \varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}\)

It turns out that the relative permittivity is related to the complex refractive index as follows:

\(n_c^2 = (n' + i\kappa)^2 = \varepsilon_r\)

The proof of the relationship between refractive index and permittivity for a standard electric wave is standard, and is in the footnote below.² And so, to change the complex refractive index, we need to change the relative permittivity of the material.

To proceed, we use an approximation. The electric displacement field is a function of the polarisation of a material. But when we mix two materials together, we can add their polarisation densities.

Before adding tartrazine, we have that water obeys

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\,\varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{water}}\,\mathbf{E} = \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{water}}\)

Then when we add the dye, we get

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{water}} + \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{tartrazine}}\)

But we know that each polarisation is proportional to the field, with its own susceptibility: P(water) = ε₀ χ(water) E and P(tartrazine) = ε₀ χ(dye) E, where χ(dye). Substituting that in, we get

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0\left(1 + \chi_w + \chi_d\right)\mathbf{E}\)

Comparing with D = ε₀εᵣE, and using that water alone has εᵣ(water) = 1 + χ(water) = n(water)², the relative permittivity of the dyed water is

\(\varepsilon_r = \varepsilon_{r,\mathrm{water}} + \chi_d = n_w^2 + \chi_d\)

For a dilute dye, χ(dye) is small compared to n(water)², so we can expand the square root and use a Taylor expansion to get the modified refractive index of the water with the dye.

\(n_c = \sqrt{n_w^2 + \chi_d} = n_w\sqrt{1 + \frac{\chi_d}{n_w^2}} \;\approx\; n_w + \frac{\chi_d}{2 n_w}\)

n_c is complex. If we write it out as n_c = n′ + iκ and split the electric susceptibility of χ(dye) that we got into real and imaginary parts, the dye shifts the real refractive index and introduces absorption by

\(\Delta n' = n' - n_w = \frac{\mathrm{Re}\,\chi_d}{2 n_w}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{\mathrm{Im}\,\chi_d}{2 n_w}\)

And putting in the Lorentz form of χ(dye) that we got earlier

\(\Delta n' = \frac{N e^2}{2 n_w \varepsilon_0 m}\,\frac{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}, \qquad \kappa = \frac{N e^2}{2 n_w \varepsilon_0 m}\,\frac{\gamma\omega}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2\omega^2}\)

For tartrazine and red light, ω is below the resonance ω₀, so ω₀² − ω² > 0 and Δn′ is positive. This means the dye raises the refractive index of the water. Meanwhile κ carries a factor of γω in the numerator and is only large near ω ≈ ω₀,, which means that we don't get absorbance.

References

Ou Z, Duh YS, Rommelfanger NJ, Keck CHC, Jiang S, Brinson K Jr, Zhao S, Schmidt EL, Wu X, Yang F, Cai B, Cui H, Qi W, Wu S, Tantry A, Roth R, Ding J, Chen X, Kaltschmidt JA, Brongersma ML, Hong G. Achieving optical transparency in live animals with absorbing molecules. Science. 2024 Sep 6;385(6713):eadm6869. doi: 10.1126/science.adm6869. Epub 2024 Sep 6. PMID: 39236186; PMCID: PMC11931656.

² Here are Maxwell's equations for electric and magnetic fields in a material. This is generated by Claude.

\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{D} = \rho_f, \qquad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}_f + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\)

\(\mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P} = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mathbf{E}, \qquad \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{H} \quad \text{(non-magnetic)}\)

The question is then - how do any of these relate to the refractive index?

No free charges or currents (ρ = 0, J = 0), non-magnetic. Faraday's law says that the curl of an electric field is the negative of the magnetic field's time derivative. Take the curl of Faraday's law, and then substitute in

\(\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\nabla \times \mathbf{B}\)

Ampère–Maxwell with J = 0:

\(\nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\)

Substitute B = μ₀H and D = ε₀E + P = ε₀εᵣE:

\(\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} + \mu_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{P}}{\partial t} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\)

This is where εᵣ enters: the polarisation current ∂P/∂t adds to the vacuum displacement current. Then (taking εᵣ constant in time, i.e. working at a single frequency)

\(\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) = -\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = -\mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}\)

\(\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) = \nabla(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}) - \nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = -\nabla^2 \mathbf{E}\)

Then if we equate both sides, we get a plane wave equation

\(\Rightarrow \quad \nabla^2 \mathbf{E} = \frac{\varepsilon_r}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}\)

Plane wave E = E₀ e^(i(kz − ωt))

\(k^2 = \varepsilon_r \frac{\omega^2}{c^2}\)

Comparing with k = (n′ + iκ) ω/c from the attenuating wave written earlier,

\(\varepsilon_r(\omega) = n_c(\omega)^2 = (n' + i\kappa)^2 = n'^2 - \kappa^2 + 2 i n' \kappa\)

URL: https://github.com/mikroverk/esp32sim, See on Hacker News

esp32sim — an ESP32 emulator in Rust: Xtensa (ESP32, S3) and RISC-V (C3, C6)

Instruction-level emulation of four ESP32 SoCs, across both of Espressif's CPU architectures. Each boots the real mask ROM, the real 2nd-stage bootloader and an unmodified application image — no patched firmware, no stubs in the way — with enough of the SoC modelled to run real projects end to end. No cloud, no accounts. MIT.

The classic ESP32 also boots its ECO3 ROM on dual LX6 cores, with GPIO, UART and timers; --board ttgo-tdisplay adds the LilyGO TTGO T-Display's ST7789 and buttons.

CPU 2 × Xtensa LX7 @ 240 MHz 1 × RISC-V RV32IMC @ 160 MHz 1 × RISC-V RV32IMAC @ 160 MHz
Command esp32sim esp32sim-c3 esp32sim-c6
Core crate xtensa-lx7 riscv-rv32 riscv-rv32 (+ the A extension)
Reported full-listing decoder checks 977 k instructions, 0 mismatches 161 k instructions, 0 mismatches 126 k instructions, 0 mismatches
Boots ROM → bootloader → FreeRTOS → app ROM → bootloader → FreeRTOS → app ROM → bootloader → FreeRTOS → app
Boards / displays ST7735, ST7701S 480×480 + touch, WS2812, camera, audio none — console only ST7789 172×320 over SPI+DMA, WS2812, an 802.15.4 energy-detect stand-in
WiFi virtual AP, WPA2, DHCP/DNS/NTP, NAT to the real network, HTTPS the same virtual AP and network: scan, WPA2, DHCP, NAT (one station) the same virtual AP and network: scan, WPA2, DHCP, NAT (one station, legacy rates)
Speed block interpreter + AArch64 JIT, ~150–240 Minsn/s plain interpreter (no block cache or JIT yet) — still well above real time on hello_world same interpreter
In the browser yes (WebAssembly) yes (WebAssembly) yes (WebAssembly)
Reported hardware comparisons JTAG trace, 8000 steps after timing-loop resynchronization console diff, 205/208 lines identical console diff, 203/204 lines identical
Status mature draft — see docs/esp32c3.md draft — see docs/esp32c6.md

These full-listing and hardware counts describe earlier manual runs. CI runs the checked-in sampled decoder corpora and emulator golden outputs; it excludes the external full-listing tests. The Xtensa objdump test excludes PIE operand comparisons. Hardware trace comparison normalizes window exceptions and resynchronizes delay loops, so it is not uninterrupted cycle-by-cycle agreement. See the test scope, CI workflow, Xtensa decoder test and hardware comparator.

Most of the SoC is shared: the C3 reuses the S3's UART, USB-Serial/JTAG, systimer, timer groups, GPIO, SPI flash controller, GDMA and SHA/AES/RSA models unchanged, and adds its own memory map, cache controller and interrupt matrix; the C6 reuses the same models again, with its own memory map, PLIC front-end, L1 cache, PCR and always-on LP blocks. Only the CPU crates are genuinely separate.

Try it in a browser, no install: https://mikroverk.github.io/esp32sim/ — Linux on the S3, the Touch-LCD-4B panel with its SID player, the pocket-tank LLM aquarium, and the C3 and C6 demos.

  wasm/           C-ABI crate wrapping all three Machines for the browser in one module
  web/            browser UI (board drawing, console, audio, camera) + emu.js/worker.js for wasm
  hw/             JTAG differential-test scripts against a real board, captured C3 and C6 consoles
  examples/       hello_world (IDF, S3, C3 and C6), waveshare-cam (autopling run script + photo),
                  wifi-station (S3), c6-wifi-station (builds for the S3, C3 and C6; the WiFi goldens'
                  firmware), c6-radio-dashboard (WiFi + 802.15.4 on the C6 board)
  tools/          PIE table generator (TRM-derived); bench.py (interleaved A/B benchmark);
                  wasm-build.sh (the WebAssembly module)

Boards (ESP32-S3)

The SoC model emits pin-level events (GPIO edges, RMT symbol streams, I2S samples); a BoardModel (esp-soc/src/board.rs) interprets them. --board atech14 (default) is the Atech 14‑port board with its ST7735, WS2812 ring, encoder and buttons; --board none is a bare module — any ESP32‑S3 firmware, console only; --board waveshare-lcd4b is the Waveshare ESP32‑S3‑Touch‑LCD‑4B (ST7701S 480×480 over the LCD_CAM RGB bus, GT911 touch, TCA9554, codecs) running the esp32-screen LVGL panel with touch; --board waveshare-amoled18-v2 is the Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-AMOLED-1.8 V2 (CO5300 368x448 over QSPI, CST820 touch); --board waveshare-cam is the Waveshare ESP32‑S3‑CAM‑OV5640 (CH32V003 IO expander, OV5640 over SCCB, ES8311/ES7210 codecs on I2C0, speaker on I2S1, OV5640 on the LCD_CAM DVP port) — runs the waveshare-autopling firmware (IDF 5.5, 16 MB flash, 8 MB octal PSRAM: --flash-mb 16 --psram-mb 8) end to end: camera frames from --cam-image or the browser (picture upload / webcam) → esp‑dl pedestrian detector on the emulated PIE SIMD unit → pling on the ES8311. See examples/waveshare-cam/. Adding a board = implementing the trait (gpio_changes, rmt_frame, i2c_devices, camera_frame, …).

The Pocket Synth firmware the atech14 demos run is its own project: atech-firmware — a PlatformIO build of the SID synth and a cRSID player for real .sid tunes. This repo carries the built images it produces, in web/wasm/fw/public/.

cargo build --release
FW=web/wasm/fw/public                       # the demo images the goldens and the web page run
./target/release/esp32sim --boot rom \
    --bootloader $FW/atech-bootloader.bin --ptable $FW/atech-ptable.bin --app $FW/atech-firmware.bin \
    --script $FW/atech-script1.txt --wav out.wav --tft-png tft.png --max-seconds 5

The mask ROM ELF is picked up from ~/.espressif/tools/esp-rom-elfs/*/esp32s3_rev0_rom.elf (shipped with ESP‑IDF). Without ESP-IDF, tools/fetch-demo-assets.sh --no-linux puts the S3, C3 and C6 ROMs in web/wasm/fw/: pass --rom web/wasm/fw/esp32s3_rev0_rom.elf, or set ESP32SIM_ROM_DIR=web/wasm/fw for the tests. --boot app skips ROM+bootloader and loads the app image directly.

A plain ESP‑IDF project, e.g. examples/hello_world (the IDF 5.5 get-started example built with idf.py set-target esp32s3 && idf.py build):

H=examples/hello_world/build
./target/release/esp32sim --board none --boot rom --console uart0 \
    --bootloader $H/bootloader/bootloader.bin --ptable $H/partition_table/partition-table.bin \
    --app $H/hello_world.bin --elf $H/hello_world.elf --elf $H/bootloader/bootloader.elf --max-seconds 26

prints the ROM banner, the bootloader and app logs on UART0, Hello world!, the countdown, and then reboots through the RTC watchdog exactly as silicon does (rst:0xc (RTC_SW_CPU_RST)), ~30× faster than real time. Chip resets (software, RTC watchdog) restart the machine from the ROM with the right reset cause; --no-reboot stops at the first reset instead.

Run — ESP32-C3

esp32sim-c3 runs unmodified ESP-IDF firmware on the emulated RISC-V core, from the real mask ROM through the real bootloader into FreeRTOS. Same flags as esp32sim (--trace, --break, --watch, --peek, --disasm, --log-periph), printing RISC-V mnemonics with symbols.

H=examples/hello_world-c3/build
./target/release/esp32sim-c3 --boot rom --flash-mb 4 \
    --bootloader $H/bootloader/bootloader.bin --ptable $H/partition_table/partition-table.bin \
    --app $H/hello_world.bin --elf $H/hello_world.elf --max-seconds 26

prints the ROM banner, the bootloader log, Hello world! and the reboot, three times over. Checked line-for-line against a physical C3 module: 205 of 208 console lines identical over three boot cycles — the difference is the ROM's Saved PC: line. --mac, --reset-cause and --strap let a run adopt a board's identity so the comparison is meaningful. WiFi station mode supports open and WPA2 virtual APs with DHCP and NAT. No boards; --boot app unsupported. See docs/esp32c3.md for what works, what does not, and the five emulator bugs the hardware found.

Run — ESP32-C6

esp32sim-c6 is the same front end on the ESP32-C6: RV32IMAC, the PLIC, a unified memory map.

H=examples/hello_world-c6/build
./target/release/esp32sim-c6 --boot rom --flash-mb 4 \
    --bootloader $H/bootloader/bootloader.bin --ptable $H/partition_table/partition-table.bin \
    --app $H/hello_world.bin --elf $H/hello_world.elf --max-seconds 27

Checked against a Waveshare ESP32-C6-LCD-1.47: 203 of 204 console lines identical over three boot cycles, including the ROM's Saved PC: after esp_restart(); the one difference is that line on the first boot. --board waveshare-c6-lcd147 adds that board — the ST7789 over SPI2 and the GDMA, the WS2812, the BOOT button — and the C6's 802.15.4 MAC answers energy scans, so the board's LVGL spectrum-scanner firmware runs end to end (examples/waveshare-c6-lcd147/). The MAC also sends and receives frames with the timing of the air, and --cooja makes the C6 an external mote of Cooja-NG, driven in exact lock-step over NDJSON (an unmodified Contiki-NG-on-IDF image exchanging broadcasts with emulated MSP430 nodes). WiFi works too: --wifi attaches the same virtual access point as on the S3 (see WiFi below). See docs/esp32c6.md.

Scripts (host actions at emulated time)

1.5  press btn1 150                       # GPIO17 low for 150 ms
2.2  knob cw 2                            # two quadrature detents on CLK5/DT4
3.4  press btn2 120
4.0  serial {"action":"set_note","value":"9"}   # into USB-CDC RX
5.0  stop

WiFi (ESP32-S3, C3, C6 and the classic ESP32)

--wifi ssid=NAME[,psk=PASS,chan=N,bssid=..] attaches a virtual access point that the unmodified Espressif WiFi blob associates with — scan, authentication, association and, with a passphrase, the WPA2-PSK four-way handshake — and a virtual network behind it (DHCP, ARP, ICMP, DNS, SNTP off the host clock). --net nat (the default) relays the guest's TCP and UDP over ordinary host sockets, so firmware reaches the real network; --net none refuses it. No firmware changes, no root, no tun device.

./target/release/esp32sim --board waveshare-lcd4b --boot rom --flash-mb 16 --psram-mb 8 \
    --bootloader $P/bootloader/bootloader.bin --ptable $P/partition_table/partition-table.bin \
    --app $P/energy_panel.bin --console usb --wifi "ssid=home,psk=secret" --max-seconds 45

runs the esp32-screen energy panel: it joins, takes a lease, syncs its clock, fetches two days of electricity prices over HTTPS and polls a real Home Assistant on the LAN. docs/networking-howto.md is the how-to (flags, debugging, limits); docs/wifi-plan.md and docs/networking-plan.md describe how the MAC model and the packet path work, and the Networking section of docs/architecture.md the layers every chip shares.

The ESP32-C6 joins the same access point and the same network, through its own MAC model (docs/wifi-c6-plan.md): one station, legacy rates, no power save. examples/c6-wifi-station is the specimen — scan, join, lease, five pings, and the state on the board's screen — and every C6 radio run needs --stub bb_init=0 (the PHY's baseband calibration wants analog hardware):

B=examples/c6-wifi-station/build-emu
./target/release/esp32sim-c6 --boot rom --flash-mb 4 --board waveshare-c6-lcd147 --console usb \
    --bootloader $B/bootloader/bootloader.bin --ptable $B/partition_table/partition-table.bin \
    --app $B/c6_wifi_station.bin --elf $B/c6_wifi_station.elf --stub bb_init=0 \
    --wifi ssid=esp32sim,psk=esp32sim-pass --max-seconds 14

The ESP32-C3 joins the same access point too, through a MAC model derived from the S3's. The same station example, built for each chip without the display, is committed under web/wasm/fw/public/ as the input of the WiFi goldens (wifi_station_{s3,c3,c6} in cli/tests/goldens.rs), so it runs without a local build:

P=web/wasm/fw/public
./target/release/esp32sim-c3 --boot rom --flash-mb 4 --console usb \
    --bootloader $P/c3-wifi-bootloader.bin --ptable $P/c3-wifi-ptable.bin --app $P/c3-wifi_station.bin \
    --wifi ssid=esp32sim,psk=esp32sim-pass --max-seconds 14

examples/c6-radio-dashboard runs WiFi and 802.15.4 energy scans in one firmware, a page each.

In the browser (WebAssembly)

tools/wasm-build.sh                  # the module -> web/wasm/esp32sim.wasm
tools/fetch-demo-assets.sh           # mask ROMs, xterm.js and the Linux image (--no-linux skips its 16 MB)
python3 -m http.server -d web 8790   # then open http://127.0.0.1:8790/?wasm&fw=hello

The demo firmware is committed; the mask ROMs, xterm.js and the Linux image are not, and every demo boots from the ROM, so run the fetch once. It gets the same files the Pages site serves.

The same emulator compiled to WebAssembly, running inside the page in a Web Worker: pick a board, load the ROM ELF and firmware from disk (or ?wasm&fw=<name> for a hosted manifest), press Boot. hello_world, the Touch-LCD-4B panel with its SID player, the Atech board, the ESP32-C3 and the ESP32-C6 all run at real time in Chrome; there is no NAT (the browser has no sockets). The S3 has a WebAssembly JIT of its own (hot blocks and regions, PIE on WASM SIMD). See docs/wasm.md. Live: https://mikroverk.github.io/esp32sim/ — Linux 6.11 on the ESP32-S3 (svermigo/Linux-on-esp32-S3, log in and type on the console), the Touch-LCD-4B panel with its SID player, the Atech board, pocket-tank (a 4-bit transformer steering the fish on the Touch-AMOLED-1.8), and the ESP32-C3 and C6 booting hello_world; or load your own firmware for any chip from disk (pick the board, or esp32c3 / esp32c6).

Debugging

--trace [--trace-from N], --break ADDR, --watch ADDR (stop when a word changes), --peek ADDR[,N], --profile (pc histogram), --log-periph (first touch of every unknown register), --stop-after-exceptions N, --gram-png (raw ST7735 GRAM), --no-jit (interpret instead of running native code — must give identical results). Env: ESP_EMU_DEBUG, ESP_EMU_DEBUG_SPI, ESP_EMU_DEBUG_USB, ESP_EMU_DEBUG_WIFI[_FRAMES], ESP_EMU_DEBUG_NET, ESP_EMU_DEBUG_AES, ESP_EMU_DEBUG_SHA, ESP_EMU_DEBUG_RSA.

Documentation

  • docs/adding.md — adding a peripheral, a board with devices, a CPU/chip, an observer

docs/ — architecture, peripheral coverage, boards, CLI reference, web UI protocol, design decisions & gotchas, roadmap, networking how-to, the WiFi and networking design notes, and the testing plan.

Provenance

Written from the ESP‑IDF register headers, the Xtensa core config shipped with ESP‑IDF, the RISC-V specification and the C3 and C6 technical reference manuals, and observed firmware behaviour. QEMU was consulted only to confirm instruction semantics (no code copied). MIT.

Differential testing against real silicon (hw/)

Every chip is checked against hardware, by different methods: the S3 in JTAG lock-step (below), the C3 and C6 by diffing a captured console against the emulator running the same binaries (hw/c3-hello-world-real.txt, 205/208 lines identical — see docs/esp32c3.md; hw/c6-hello-world-real.txt, 203/204 — see docs/esp32c6.md). Those comparisons found five emulator bugs each, including a device-command race and a cycle counter that did not restart at reset — neither of which a board-free test would have caught.

ESP32-S3, JTAG lock-step

DIFF_DIR=hw/<board> FLASH_MB=8 hw/difftest.sh 3000 — the scripts read efuses/strap from the attached chip over JTAG, then step it and the emulator in lock-step on the same flash dump (flash-8M.bin if present). Atech board, 2026-08-25: 3000 steps from reset, 0 divergences.

Any ESP32‑S3 board on USB works (its built‑in USB‑Serial/JTAG carries both the console and JTAG). The flow, all scripted:

# one-time: dump the board's bootloader/partition table/app start (esptool) into hw/flash-0-1M.bin
hw/difftest.sh 8000                 # reset → single-step 8000 instructions on the chip and in the emulator, diff
hw/difftest-at.sh 403c8948 6000     # run both to a PC (here the 2nd-stage bootloader entry), then step 6000 and diff

difftest*.sh read the chip's efuses (hw/efuse.txt), strapping pins and the peripheral reset state (hw/reset-regs.txt, dumped over JTAG at reset halt) and start the emulator from the same image and state. hw/compare.py diffs pc a0..a15 ps windowbase per instruction, masks PS.INTLEVEL (forced during single‑step), hides window‑exception handlers (the debugger steps over them atomically) and resynchronises across CCOUNT‑timed delay loops, which iterate a different number of times when each step takes milliseconds.

Result so far: the ROM reset path (8000 steps) and 3000+ steps of the IDF 5.5 bootloader run with zero PC divergence; remaining register differences are RTC‑domain values that depend on the previous boot.

Live board UI (ESP32-S3)

./target/release/esp32sim --boot rom --bootloader … --ptable … --app … --web 8766
# open http://127.0.0.1:8766/

--web PORT runs the emulator in real time and serves web/run.html: the 14‑port board (knob + LED ring, buttons, speaker VU, the ST7735 in its physical orientation plus a readable copy), USB‑CDC and UART0 consoles, an action box for the SDK JSON protocol, and audio through WebAudio. Inputs: click the buttons, wheel/drag/←→ on the knob, click the cap to push it.

Performance / real time (ESP32-S3)

Blocks of instructions are decoded once and executed from a cache, then compiled to native AArch64 code (--no-jit falls back to the interpreter and must give identical results); idle cores (waiti) are skipped, device time is delivered lazily against computed timer deadlines, and interrupt lines are recomputed only when a source changes. See docs/speed-plan.md for the measurements behind each step. The Pocket Synth firmware runs at real time with margin while idle or playing notes; the one place it cannot keep up is a full display redraw, where core 1 runs 100 % busy bit‑banging SPI (4.8 M instructions per 20 ms — 240 Minsn/s needed, ~70 Minsn/s achieved on an M‑series MacBook). Each redraw therefore costs ~0.3 s of lag, which the UI's adaptive audio buffer absorbs (it grows on underrun, up to 400 ms) and the pacer recovers afterwards; if the emulator ever falls more than 0.5 s behind it resynchronises instead of bursting. The header shows real time, ⚠ N s behind and the resync count.

ESP_EMU_RT_LOG=1 prints every 20 ms window that took > 40 ms wall with both cores' instruction counts and PCs. hw/wsdrive.py [port] [seconds] drives the UI protocol without a browser (button presses + knob turns) and reports push gaps, lag and audio delivered — use it to measure changes to the scheduler.

Contributing

Contributions are welcome. CONTRIBUTING.md lists the checks a pull request needs (the same ones CI runs) and the conventions for tests, experiments and evidence.

License

esp32sim is released under the MIT License, copyright Joakim Eriksson (@joakimeriksson), Alice (@aliceisjustplaying), and (@mfiumara) Mattia Fiumara.

Third-party code, data and demo files keep their own licenses:

  • pocket-tank (mediacutlet/pocket-tank, MIT). Its bootloader, partition table and app are committed under web/wasm/fw/public/ with pocket-tank-LICENSE.txt; its model is fetched.
  • MicroPython (micropython.org, MIT): the official ESP32_GENERIC v1.29.0 image of the T-Display demo, fetched by tools/fetch-micropython.sh, not committed; the demo's app and filesystem are in examples/ttgo-tdisplay with Russ Hughes's st7789py driver and fonts (MIT), notice in web/wasm/fw/public/tdisplay-NOTICE.txt.
  • Mask ROM ELFs (espressif/esp-rom-elfs, Apache-2.0), fetched, not committed.
  • xterm.js (xtermjs/xterm.js, MIT), fetched, not committed.
  • Linux image (svermigo/Linux-on-esp32-S3, GPL-3.0), fetched, not committed.
  • ESP-IDF ADC calibration data (Espressif, Apache-2.0): the curve-fitting coefficients and S3 ADC1 calibration from #165, now together in esp-periph/src/sar_adc.rs; see esp-periph/LICENSE-ADC.

item.title: MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood (256 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.engadget.com/2288729/mapquest-will-now-show-you-where-flock-cameras-are-in-your-neighborhood/, See on Hacker News

You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the app.

Matthew G Eddy/Shutterstock

MapQuest has been on quite the unexpected tear over the last couple of months. The mapping service's app surged in popularity after it refused to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America (unlike Google Maps and Apple Maps). MapQuest also added useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions.

The app now has another handy tool. You can toggle a layer that shows known outdoor surveillance cameras and license plate readers.

The layer will show you where Flock cameras are. It also displays the locations of cameras from the likes of Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia and Verkada. The layer sits alongside options to view traffic and incidents, so it should be easy to find in the app.

MapQuest announced the update with a short video that's set to Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me." Chef's kiss, no notes.

You might not be able to easily avoid these cameras on your commute or other usual routes, but the layer may be helpful in illustrating how pervasive these things are in your area. It's useful information to have for those who are trying to rid their neighborhoods of surveillance cams.

item.title: Israeli settlers attack olive framers & Washington Post journalist in West Bank (139 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/16/israeli-settlers-attack-olive-farmers-west-bank-washington-post-journalist-heidi-levine, See on Hacker News

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in West Bank towns on Friday. Palestinian authorities said they recorded attacks in eight villages, and injuries among at least 20 people.

It was the latest series of attacks in a deadly campaign of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in recent months, violence which has drawn accusations of “ethnic cleansing”, including from the British government.

In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, at least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.

In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that the facts surrounding the attack on Levine were “unclear”, suggesting the attack was the fault of “200 Arabs and far-left activists” who confronted Israeli youths. The office added that it condemned “violence against anyone”.

There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.

Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but there has been a rise in violence this year as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.

At least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 others injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without the approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.

Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.

Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.

Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.

Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.

Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.

A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

item.title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour (181 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03266-x, See on Hacker News

Scientists have rapidly restored bleached coral in a laboratory by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment, giving hope for reversing widespread coral decline.

Rising sea temperatures are stressing corals, causing the animals to expel the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues and give them their colour — a process known as bleaching. Because the photosynthetic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) provide corals with most of their nutrients, without them, the marine organisms are likely to starve and die.

A team of researchers has now shown that it is possible to fully reverse this bleaching process, in just days. It reported the findings in Science Advances on 14 October1.

“This incredible new result — that fast and full recovery is possible in bleached coral — can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a marine ecologist at Stanford University’s Center for Ocean Solutions in California and a co-author on the study.

The healing touch

In early 2025, marine scientist, and study co-author, Stephen Palumbi at Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, was working in the lab and noticed that two coral fragments in a tank were accidentally touching. Where the healthy and bleached fragment met, colour had begun to seep into the ghostly branch. “I’d never seen that before,” he remembers.

Danny Collins, who was studying how disease spreads through coral contact as part of his PhD at Stanford, set out to investigate whether algae can also spread and, if so, how.

He prepared ten pairs of coral fragments from the same animal (Pocillopora damicornis)., Each pair had a bleached and a healthy fragment. He set up five pairs so that their fragments touched each other, and five with their fragments separated by a few millimetres. In the touching pairs, the bleached coral recovered within eight weeks.

“We were blown away when we watched the colour of the algal symbionts transfer over to the bleached coral, reviving it in a very short period of time,” Collins says. By week two, the symbiont population was doubling every four days, which is much faster than the recovery times seen in studies of coral recovering naturally in the wild2,3.

After touching the healthy fragment for a week, a bleached branch could fully recover on its own, even if separated from the healthy branch.

In the slightly separated pairs, the bleached fragments died after 20 weeks.

Using high-powered microscopy, the team showed that two coral fragments fuse together by creating a tissue bridge — enabling symbiont transfer. This only occurred for coral fragments taken from an individual of the same genetic make-up, called a genet. Fragments from different species and even different animals of the same species did not fuse together, and so did not nurse the bleached piece back to health.
